cues.text: A Church Entangled with the Old Regime

On the eve of 1789, the Catholic Church in France owned roughly a tenth of the nation's land, collected its own tithes, and stood deeply woven into a monarchy groaning under debt and popular resentment.
When the Bastille fell that July, revolutionaries turned quickly from reforming abuses to dismantling the Church's independence altogether, nationalizing her property within months.
We recognize a temptation as old as Christendom itself in this collapse: a Church too comfortable in worldly privilege is often the one least prepared for the trial that follows.
The Civil Constitution of the Clergy

In 1790, the National Assembly passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy , reorganizing every French diocese and parish as an arm of the state and demanding all clergy swear a civil oath of loyalty above their loyalty to Rome.
Roughly half of France's priests, the refractory clergy , refused, choosing exile, hiding, or death over the oath; those who complied became known as constitutional or juring priests.
The divide split parishes down the middle and marked the moment persecution turned from confiscation to outright war against conscience itself.
The September Massacres
As foreign armies threatened Paris in the late summer of 1792 , revolutionary mobs broke into the city's overcrowded prisons.
Over several days, they slaughtered more than a thousand inmates, among them some two hundred priests and three bishops held simply for refusing the civil oath.
The September Martyrs , as they came to be known, were among the first mass killings of clergy in the revolution's descent into terror.
What had begun as legal harassment had, within three years, become naked massacre.
The Cult of Reason
By 1793, the revolutionary government moved beyond persecuting individual clergy toward erasing Christian worship itself.

The Gregorian calendar was abolished, Sunday was suppressed as a day of rest, and on November 10, 1793, Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris was rededicated as a Temple of Reason, its altar replaced by an actress portraying the goddess Liberty.
Churches nationwide were looted, crosses torn down, and priests pressured to marry or renounce their vocations publicly.
An estimated thirty thousand priests fled France altogether rather than comply, while thousands more who stayed were imprisoned, deported to penal colonies, or killed.
Sixteen Carmelites of Compiègne

Among the persecution's most enduring witnesses were the Discalced Carmelite nuns of Compiègne, expelled from their convent in 1792 but who continued living in secret community until their arrest in June 1794.
Tried before the Revolutionary Tribunal on trumped-up charges of "fanaticism," the sixteen women comprised eleven choir nuns, three lay sisters, and two externs.
They renewed their religious vows at the foot of the scaffold and mounted it one by one on July 17, 1794 , singing the Veni Creator Spiritus and the Psalms until the last voice fell silent.

Their prioress, Mother Teresa of St. Augustine , had offered their community's lives as a sacrifice for an end to the bloodshed; ten days later, the architect of the Terror, Robespierre , himself went to the guillotine.
The Terror's Collapse

Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor (July 27, 1794) broke the machinery of the Terror almost overnight, and organized dechristianization gradually eased in the years that followed, though sporadic persecution and confiscation continued under the Directory.
Full reconciliation between the French state and the Church did not arrive until Napoleon's Concordat of 1801 restored Catholic worship as the religion of the majority of the French people.
By then, tens of thousands of priests, religious, and lay faithful had been killed, exiled, or driven underground for a single unyielding refusal: to place the state above the Church of Christ.
Legacy
The sixteen Carmelites of Compiègne were beatified in 1906 by Pope St. Pius X and canonized by Pope Francis in 2024.

Their story, along with that of the Church's other revolutionary martyrs, has inspired countless meditations on the redemptive power of a freely offered life, most famously Georges Bernanos's Dialogues of the Carmelites .
The French Revolution's assault on the Church still speaks to every generation tempted to believe that a state can simply legislate faith out of existence.
It could confiscate buildings, silence bells, and fill the Seine with the blood of the faithful, but it could not, in the end, stop sixteen women from singing on their way to God.
